section.title: The Siege of Samaria
section.sectionRationale: Ben-hadad besieges Samaria until famine drives its people to horrifying extremes, and the king, blaming Elisha and the LORD, vows the prophet's death. Elisha announces impossible abundance within a day, an officer scoffs, and four desperate lepers discover the LORD has routed the entire Aramean army by sound alone, leaving the camp intact for Israel's plunder. The prophecy is fulfilled to the letter, including the scoffing officer's own death.
section.thesis: When the LORD's people are reduced to unthinkable horror by siege and famine, the LORD alone can turn desperate scarcity into sudden abundance overnight, and His spoken word through His prophet is fulfilled exactly, both in blessing for the humble and in judgment for the one who doubted.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the siege, famine, and the king's fury against Elisha, 6:24 to 33; Elisha's prophecy of plenty and the officer's scoffing, 7:1 to 2; the lepers discover the abandoned camp, 7:3 to 15; and the prophecy fulfilled to the letter, 7:16 to 20.

units.label: Siege, famine, and the king's fury
units.note: we boiled my son and ate him

verses.text: Some time later, Ben-hadad king of Aram assembled his entire army and marched up to besiege Samaria.

So there was a great {{raab|famine}} in Samaria. Indeed, they besieged the city so long that a donkey's head sold for eighty shekels of silver, and a quarter cab of dove's dung sold for five shekels of silver.
As the king of Israel was passing by on the wall, a woman cried out to him, "Help me, my lord the king!"
He answered, "If the LORD does not help you, where can I find help for you? From the threshing floor or the winepress?"
Then the king asked her, "What is the matter?" And she answered, "This woman said to me, 'Give up your son, that we may eat him, and tomorrow we will eat my son.'
So we boiled my son and ate him, and the next day I said to her, 'Give up your son, that we may eat him.' But she had hidden her son."
When the king heard the words of the woman, he tore his clothes. And as he passed by on the wall, the people saw the sackcloth under his clothes next to his skin.
He announced, "May God punish me, and ever so severely, if the head of Elisha son of Shaphat remains on his shoulders through this day!"

Now Elisha was sitting in his house, and the elders were sitting with him. The king sent a messenger ahead, but before he arrived, Elisha said to the elders, "Do you see how this murderer has sent someone to cut off my head? Look, when the messenger comes, shut the door to keep him out. Is not the sound of his master's footsteps behind him?"
While Elisha was still speaking with them, the messenger came down to him. And the king said, "This calamity is from the LORD. Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?"

units.label: Elisha's prophecy and the officer's scorn
units.note: you will see it with your own eyes, but you will not eat any of it

verses.text: Then Elisha said, "Hear the word of the LORD! This is what the LORD says: 'About this time tomorrow at the gate of Samaria, a {{seah|seah}} of fine flour will sell for a shekel, and two seahs of barley will sell for a shekel.'"

But the officer on whose arm the king leaned answered the man of God, "Look, even if the LORD were to make windows in heaven, could this really happen?" "You will see it with your own eyes," replied Elisha, "but you will not eat any of it."

units.label: The lepers discover the abandoned camp
units.note: today is a day of good news

verses.text: Now there were four men with leprosy at the entrance of the city gate, and they said to one another, "Why just sit here until we die?

If we say, 'Let us go into the city,' we will die there from the famine in the city; but if we sit here, we will also die. So come now, let us go over to the camp of the Arameans. If they let us live, we will live; if they kill us, we will die."
So they arose at twilight and went to the camp of the Arameans. But when they came to the outskirts of the camp, there was not a man to be found.

For the Lord had caused the Arameans to hear the {{qol|sound}} of chariots, horses, and a great army, so that they said to one another, "Look, the king of Israel must have hired the kings of the Hittites and Egyptians to attack us."
Thus the Arameans had arisen and fled at twilight, abandoning their tents and horses and donkeys. The camp was intact, and they had run for their lives.

When the lepers reached the edge of the camp, they went into a tent to eat and drink. Then they carried off the silver, gold, and clothing, and went and hid them. On returning, they entered another tent, carried off some items from there, and hid them.

Finally, they said to one another, "We are not doing what is right. Today is a day of {{besorah|good news}}. If we are silent and wait until morning light, our sin will overtake us. Now, therefore, let us go and tell the king's household."
So they went and called out to the gatekeepers of the city, saying, "We went to the Aramean camp and no one was there, not a trace, only tethered horses and donkeys, and the tents were intact."
The gatekeepers shouted the news, and it was reported to the king's household.

So the king got up in the night and said to his servants, "Let me tell you what the Arameans have done to us. They know we are starving, so they have left the camp to hide in the field, thinking, 'When they come out of the city, we will take them alive and enter the city.'"

But one of his servants replied, "Please, have scouts take five of the horses that remain in the city. Their plight will be no worse than all the Israelites who are left here. You can see that all the Israelites here are doomed. So let us send them and find out."
Then the scouts took two chariots with horses, and the king sent them after the Aramean army, saying, "Go and see."
And they tracked them as far as the Jordan, and indeed, the whole way was littered with the clothing and equipment the Arameans had thrown off in haste. So the scouts returned and told the king.

units.label: The prophecy fulfilled to the letter
units.note: just as the man of God had told the king

verses.text: Then the people went out and plundered the camp of the Arameans. It was then that a seah of fine flour sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley sold for a shekel, according to the word of the LORD.

Now the king had appointed the officer on whose arm he leaned to be in charge of the gate, but the people trampled him in the gateway, and he died, just as the man of God had foretold when the king had come to him.
It happened just as the man of God had told the king: "About this time tomorrow at the gate of Samaria, two seahs of barley will sell for a shekel, and a seah of fine flour will sell for a shekel."

And the officer had answered the man of God, "Look, even if the LORD were to make windows in heaven, could this really happen?" So Elisha had replied, "You will see it with your own eyes, but you will not eat any of it!"
And that is just what happened to him. The people trampled him in the gateway, and he died.

raab.gloss: Famine. The siege drives Samaria's famine to such extremes that a donkey's head and even dove's dung become traded commodities, and two mothers resort to devouring their own sons, fulfilling the horrifying covenant warnings of Deuteronomy 28:53-57 against persistent unfaithfulness.

seah.gloss: A dry measure of roughly 7.3 liters. Elisha's prophecy that a seah of fine flour would sell for a mere shekel the very next day, after famine prices had spiraled to nearly unthinkable extremes, promised a reversal so drastic that the king's own officer could not believe it.

qol.gloss: Sound or voice. The LORD caused the Arameans to hear a qol of chariots, horses, and a great army, though no such army was actually present, routing an entire besieging force through sound alone and proving that He needs no visible weapon to accomplish deliverance.

besorah.gloss: Good news or glad tidings, the same word family later used for gospel, the good news of Christ. The lepers' insistence that they must not keep this besorah to themselves models the instinct that good news, once received, demands to be shared rather than hoarded.

basic.context: Ben-hadad's siege reduces Samaria to unthinkable famine, driving two women to an act of cannibalism that horrifies even the king, who blames Elisha and the LORD and vows to kill the prophet. Elisha, unmoved, announces that within a day prices will collapse from famine extremes to ordinary abundance, a promise so unbelievable that the king's own officer mocks it. That very night, unseen by anyone, the LORD causes the besieging Aramean army to hear the sound of a massive approaching force and flee in panic, abandoning a fully stocked camp. Four desperate lepers, expecting only death, discover the empty camp, feast, then responsibly report the good news, leading Israel to plunder unimaginable abundance exactly as Elisha foretold, down to the scoffing officer's own death.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative describing a specific siege, famine, and deliverance; it is not a promise that every crisis will resolve overnight or that skeptics will always meet a literal, immediate downfall. What endures is the LORD's power to reverse the most desperate circumstances instantly and completely, and the certainty that His spoken word, whether of blessing or of warning, comes to pass exactly as declared.
basic.originalLanguages: The raab, famine, described here fulfills the terrifying covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28, yet even here Elisha promises reversal: a seah of flour, an ordinary measure, restored to ordinary prices within a day. The LORD accomplishes deliverance merely by causing the enemy to hear a qol, sound, of a phantom army, no battle required. The lepers cannot keep the besorah, good news, to themselves, an instinct the gospel itself will later require of all who receive it.
basic.typology: Deliverance accomplished entirely by the LORD without a single Israelite sword raised anticipates the pattern of salvation by grace, won by God's own action rather than human effort, discovered first by society's outcasts, the lepers, who then cannot help but share the good news with others.
basic.christ: The lepers, themselves ritually excluded and expecting nothing but death, are the first to discover and receive the sudden abundance, and their insistence on sharing the good news anticipates how the gospel of Christ is first received by the humble and outcast, who then cannot keep silent, Luke 4:18, 1 Corinthians 1:26-29. The unbelieving officer who sees the miracle yet is trampled before tasting it pictures the danger of witnessing God's grace without ever partaking of it by faith.
basic.god: God can turn the most desperate scarcity into sudden abundance without any human effort, showing His power is not limited by circumstances however extreme. He also holds His word utterly reliable, both to bless the humble sufferers and to bring exactly the judgment He speaks upon willful unbelief, refusing to let either promise fall to the ground unfulfilled.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 28:53-57 foretold the horrifying famine cannibalism now literally fulfilled in Samaria's siege, the covenant curse for persistent unfaithfulness. Isaiah 37:36 records another besieging army routed by the LORD without a battle, the same pattern of deliverance without human combat. Hebrews 3:12-19 warns against the unbelief the officer displayed, seeing but never truly trusting.
basic.oneStory: From the depths of covenant judgment, cannibalism under siege, the LORD brings sudden, total deliverance discovered first by society's outcasts, who cannot keep the news to themselves, while the one who saw but never believed is destroyed exactly as warned, a pattern that anticipates the gospel: grace received by the humble, judgment falling on unbelief that witnesses but never trusts.

context.literary:
This passage uses a device the narrator applies nowhere else in Kings quite so insistently, verbatim repetition. Elisha's prophecy in 7:1, a seah of fine flour will sell for a shekel, is repeated almost word for word as fulfilled in 7:16, and both the prophecy and the officer's scorn are quoted a third time in 7:18-19 before his death is narrated a second time in 7:20, having already been reported once in 7:17. Nothing in this stretch happens only once, everything is spoken, then fulfilled, then reviewed in a doubled account that leaves no room to call it coincidence.

The passage is also framed by two scenes of direct, desperate speech from society's least powerful people. A nameless woman cries out, help me, my lord the king, from inside the starving city, 6:26, and her horrifying account triggers the king's fury against Elisha. Four nameless lepers debate aloud outside the gate, why sit here until we die, 7:3-4, and their decision triggers the discovery of Israel's deliverance. Between these two speeches sits the hinge of the whole account, Elisha's two verse announcement, 7:1-2, that within a single day the horror of the first scene will give way entirely to the abundance of the second.

The narrative also withholds information deliberately. Readers learn that the camp is empty only when the lepers do, 7:5, even though the cause of the Aramean flight, a sound the LORD caused them to hear, 7:6, is disclosed to the reader in the very next breath, so that the king's own scouts must independently verify what the reader already knows, 7:14-15, a doubled confirmation matching the doubled fulfillment of the prophecy that follows it.
context.historical:
This is not the first time Ben-hadad's forces had besieged this city, 1 Kings 20:1 records an earlier siege of Samaria under Ahab that Israel actually survived by battle, which makes the total helplessness of this second siege, no battle is even attempted, all the more striking. Samaria sat on a defensible hill, well fortified enough that Aram could not simply storm it and instead settled in for a blockade long enough to starve the population into the horrors the text records, a common and deliberately slow siege tactic across the ancient world.

The famine prices, a donkey's head for eighty shekels of silver and a small measure of dove's dung for five, mark the total collapse of ordinary trade, items normally discarded or unclean becoming currency worthy commodities. The king's sackcloth worn under his royal robes, next to his skin, 6:30, was a genuine penitential practice, worn secretly against the body rather than displayed, suggesting private grief rather than public performance. The officer on whose arm the king leaned, a real court post for a trusted attendant, is given command of the gate once the crisis passes, 7:17, the natural place to station an officer since city gates doubled as marketplaces where grain prices like the ones Elisha named would actually be set and paid.

Famine driven cannibalism, horrifying as it is, is not confined to this account in the ancient world's own record of extended sieges, and Scripture itself records the identical horror recurring later at Jerusalem's own final fall, a detail that underlines how real and how repeatable this particular curse proved to be for a covenant people who persisted in unfaithfulness.
context.canonical:
This siege fulfills Deuteronomy 28:53-57 almost to the letter, the covenant curse warning that a besieged people would eat the flesh of their own children, spoken by Moses centuries earlier as the outer edge of what covenant unfaithfulness would bring upon Israel. That the fulfillment falls on Samaria under a king who blames Elisha rather than his own nation's persistent idolatry, 6:31, 33, shows a people who have reached the curse's horror without yet reaching the repentance Moses attached hope to, Deuteronomy 30:1-3.

The horror does not stay confined to the northern kingdom either. Centuries later, when Jerusalem itself finally falls to Babylon, the same unthinkable act recurs, the hands of compassionate women have cooked their own children, Lamentations 4:10, and the famine in the city was so severe that the people of the land had no food, 2 Kings 25:3, proving that the warning first fulfilled here at Samaria was never limited to one city or one generation of unfaithfulness.

The deliverance itself belongs to a wider biblical pattern of enemies routed without a single Israelite blow struck, a pattern that recurs on a still larger scale when the LORD strikes down a hundred and eighty five thousand Assyrians besieging Jerusalem in a single night, 2 Kings 19:35, and Sennacherib withdraws without ever renewing the attack, 2 Kings 19:36. Later still, the lepers who receive this good news first anticipate the pattern Jesus deliberately repeats, announcing that the poor have good news preached to them, Luke 4:18, precisely the people this world counts last.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wants readers to see two kinds of seeing collide. The king assumes the empty Aramean camp must be a trap, reasoning from ordinary military logic, they know we are starving, so they have left the camp to hide in the field, 7:12, and requires scouts to test that theory before he will act on the good news reported to him, 7:13-14. The four lepers, by contrast, act immediately on what they themselves discover, we are not doing right by staying silent, 7:9, without waiting for any official confirmation at all. The narrative deliberately rewards the lepers' plain trust over the king's calculated caution, since both groups reach the same true conclusion, but only one group reaches it first and acts on it.

The doubled, verbatim fulfillment of Elisha's prophecy also serves a specific polemical aim within the larger Elisha cycle, proving that the prophetic word carries more reliable authority than either royal policy or trained military assessment. An officer close enough to the king to lean on his arm, a man whose judgement the king evidently trusted in matters of state, is shown to be entirely wrong about what God can do, while a captive, unnamed prophet's word about grain prices at a city gate comes true to the shekel. Original hearers living under kings whose own competence they had reason to doubt were meant to relocate their confidence accordingly.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This is a single historical siege, famine, and deliverance, not a template guaranteeing that every crisis will resolve within a fixed twenty four hours, nor a claim that every skeptic who doubts God's word will meet a literal, visible death as a direct result. The specific timeframe, prices, and even the manner of the officer's death describe what happened on this occasion, at this gate, to this man, not a formula transferable to other circumstances by name.

What the passage does carry forward is confidence in the character behind the event, a God who can reverse total, covenant curse level scarcity completely and without human effort, and a seriousness about unbelief that witnesses grace up close yet refuses to trust it enough to act. Readers are not meant to expect an identical twenty four hour reversal of their own crises, but they are meant to take seriously that God's spoken word, whether of blessing or of warning, is never merely decorative and always comes to pass.

debates.question: Why did the king blame Elisha and the LORD for the famine rather than Ben-hadad's siege, 6:31, 33?

views.label: Misdirected anger reflecting a fundamentally faithless heart
views.case: The king's fury at Elisha, despite Elisha having repeatedly protected Israel from Aramean ambush in the previous chapter, 6:9-10, exposes a deeper unbelief already present in Israel's leadership, blaming God's messenger rather than repenting of the persistent unfaithfulness that had brought this covenant judgment in the first place.

views.label: Genuine despair after years of compounding national crisis
views.case: By this point Israel had suffered ongoing Aramean aggression across several chapters, and the king's exasperated cry, why should I wait for the LORD any longer, may reflect the raw despair of a man who has run out of strength rather than settled theological rebellion, a despair Elisha's prophecy immediately answers with grace rather than condemnation.

debates.bearing: Either way, Elisha's calm response and immediate prophecy of overnight deliverance shows that the LORD's mercy was not withdrawn even from a faithless king and a despairing, cursing nation, answering unbelief with abundant, entirely undeserved grace.

debates.question: Was the officer's death by trampling, 7:17, 20, a direct act of divine judgment or simply the natural outcome of a chaotic crowd at a gate?

views.label: A direct, foreordained sentence carried out to the letter
views.case: The narrator states twice, and precisely as the man of God had foretold, framing the death not as an unfortunate accident but as the specific fulfillment of a specific prophetic word, spoken as judgment for treating the LORD's power as impossible even when told plainly it would happen.

views.label: Accurate foreknowledge of an entirely natural event
views.case: Nothing in the text describes God striking the officer directly, only a foreseeable outcome of stationing a single officer to control a starving, surging crowd rushing toward sudden abundance at his own gate, so the miracle lies in Elisha's foreknowledge rather than in any special act of divine violence against the man.

debates.bearing: Either reading treats the outcome as a real and precise fulfillment of Elisha's word rather than coincidence, and both agree that seeing a promise proven true is never the same thing as trusting it enough to act, which is exactly what cost the officer his place at the feast he had lived to see.

study.originalLanguages:
Elisha's prophecy in 7:1, about this time tomorrow, translates ka'et machar, a phrase Scripture reserves for moments of decisive, dated divine action. The LORD uses the identical construction to warn Pharaoh of the coming hail, at this time tomorrow I will rain down the worst hail that has ever fallen on Egypt, Exodus 9:18, and to tell Samuel that at this time tomorrow he would send the man who would save Israel from the Philistines, 1 Samuel 9:16. Elisha's announcement borrows the exact idiom Scripture already uses for God's most consequential, publicly falsifiable interventions.

The officer's scoffing question, even if the LORD were to make windows in heaven, 7:2 and again 7:19, uses arubot, windows or floodgates, the same rare word that describes the floodgates of the heavens opened at the flood, Genesis 7:11, and, on the opposite end of Scripture's use of the term, the windows of heaven the LORD promises to open with blessing without measure for a faithful, tithing people, Malachi 3:10. The officer reaches for the one image in Hebrew that Scripture elsewhere uses both for judgment poured out and for blessing poured out, and mockingly assumes it can only ever mean the first.

The word rendered officer, both for the man at the gate and, later, the man appointed over it, is shalish, a specific military term for an elite attendant standing close enough to a king or commander to be trusted with his own safety, related to the same root behind the title given to David's most honoured fighting men, the Three, 2 Samuel 23:8. That a man of this rank and trust is the one who cannot believe a plain prophetic word sharpens the irony, worldly proximity to power is no substitute for simple faith.

Finally, the raab, famine, that opens this passage is the same word used of the famine that once drove Joseph's brothers to Egypt for grain, Genesis 41:56-57, and that Joseph later tells them God had turned to a great deliverance, Genesis 45:5-8. The same word for total scarcity recurs across Scripture attached again and again to stories where the LORD's reversal, not human foresight, turns out to be Israel's actual rescue.

The measure Elisha names, a seah, is deliberately ordinary rather than extraordinary, a common unit of dry goods any household would recognise, which is precisely the point. The prophecy does not promise a strange new abundance never seen before, only a return to the plain, unremarkable prices that had existed before the siege began, which is exactly why the officer finds it so hard to credit, he cannot imagine that rescue could be this simple, this near, and this soon.

typology.type: Total deliverance achieved without a single blow struck by Israel, 7:5-7
typology.fulfillment: The Aramean army flees a sound with no army behind it, and Israel does nothing at all to earn or accomplish its own rescue. This anticipates salvation accomplished entirely by God's own action, apart from human effort, Ephesians 2:8-9, and echoes Moses' word to a helpless Israel at the sea, the LORD will fight for you, you need only to be still, Exodus 14:14. The type is not exact, since Israel's escape from Aram left the surrounding crisis of unbelief untouched, while the salvation Christ accomplishes changes the heart of those it rescues.

typology.type: Outcasts, the lepers, first discovering and unable to withhold good news, 7:3-10
typology.fulfillment: Four men excluded from ordinary community life are the first to find, taste, and then insist on sharing the abundance meant for the whole city. This anticipates the gospel first received by, and proclaimed through, the humble and overlooked, Luke 4:18, and Jesus' own pattern of eating with those the religious establishment refused to touch. The correspondence has limits, the lepers act partly from self interested conscience, our sin will overtake us, 7:9, while the gospel's messengers are moved chiefly by love rather than fear of exposure.

typology.type: Extreme scarcity reversed overnight into abundance at the very gate of the city, 7:1, 16
typology.fulfillment: Famine prices collapse to ordinary, even generous, levels within a single day, a total and instant reversal rather than a slow recovery. This anticipates the banquet the LORD of Hosts will prepare for all peoples, a feast of aged wine and choice meat, Isaiah 25:6, and the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9, where scarcity gives way permanently rather than for one season. The type is partial, since Samaria's abundance was temporary and local, while the feast it anticipates never runs out and excludes no nation that will come.

typology.type: An officer who sees the fulfilled promise yet is barred from tasting it, 7:17-20
typology.fulfillment: The one man stationed to witness the miracle up close, appointed over the very gate where the abundance is sold, dies before he can eat any of it, exactly as foretold. This anticipates the wilderness generation who saw the LORD's glory and his signs yet were barred from entering the land because they tested him and disobeyed, Numbers 14:22-23, and Jesus' warning that many will come from east and west to share the banquet while the sons of the kingdom are shut outside, Matthew 8:11-12. Nearness to a fulfilled promise, in each case, is shown to be no substitute for trusting it.

study.christ:
This passage leads to Christ first by the shape of the rescue itself. Israel does nothing to end the siege, no soldier is armed, no strategy devised, the LORD alone causes an entire army to hear a sound and flee, 7:6-7. That total passivity in the face of an impossible threat anticipates Moses' word to a trapped, defenceless Israel at the sea, the LORD will fight for you, you need only to be still, Exodus 14:14, and finds its fullest gospel expression in salvation that is by grace through faith, not of works, so that no one can boast, Ephesians 2:8-9. What Samaria could not do for itself, and what no sinner can do for themselves, God accomplishes entirely alone.

It leads to Christ by the order in which grace arrives. Four lepers, excluded from the city and expected only to die, are the very first to taste the abundance the whole population had been longing for, and the very ones who insist it must be shared rather than hoarded. Centuries later Jesus announces his mission in words that name exactly this kind of person first, good news to the poor, release to the captives, Luke 4:18, and eats deliberately with the very people this world had already decided to sit outside the gate.

It leads to Christ by warning as much as by promise. The officer sees the miracle with his own eyes, stands close enough to oversee its distribution, and still does not live to taste it, precisely because he had refused to believe the word before it happened. Jesus later describes exactly this danger, many will come from the east and the west to share the banquet, but the sons of the kingdom will be thrown outside, Matthew 8:11-12, a warning that proximity to a fulfilled promise, even eyewitness proximity, saves no one who will not trust it.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The specific price of flour, the number of lepers, and the exact hour of the officer's death are the concrete furniture of a real, dated event, not a hidden code for the gospel. What the passage supplies is the shape of a rescue accomplished entirely by God, received first by the least likely people, and refused, to his own ruin, by a man who watched it happen and still would not believe it.
study.god:
This passage shows a God who delivers before anyone has repented. The king's last recorded word before Elisha's prophecy is total renunciation, this calamity is from the LORD, why should I wait for the LORD any longer, 6:33, and the very next verse is not rebuke but rescue, hear the word of the LORD, 7:1. Grace here precedes and provokes faith rather than waiting to reward it, since nothing in the surrounding narrative records repentance before the famine breaks.

He is a God who works on the unseen side of every crisis as freely as on the visible side. Just as he once opened a servant's eyes to see an army of fire, he here causes an entire besieging army to hear the sound of chariots, horses, and a great army that was never actually there, 7:6, turning their own fear into the very mechanism of Israel's rescue without a single Israelite even knowing what was happening until morning.

He is also a God whose spoken word carries the same weight whether it promises blessing or warns of judgment. A seah of flour will sell for a shekel, and it does. You will see it with your own eyes but not eat any of it, and the officer does not. Nothing in this passage suggests God's promises are more reliable than his warnings, or that either can be waited out, mocked, or verified into irrelevance, both come to pass down to the smallest detail.

And he is a God who reverses the deepest curse a covenant people can suffer, siege cannibalism, the exact horror Moses had warned would follow persistent unfaithfulness, and does so completely, within a single day, and at the hands of society's most despised members. His mercy in this passage is not partial or gradual, it is as total as the judgment it answers.

Finally, this is a God who lets ordinary human channels, gatekeepers, scouts, a king's own household, carry news that he alone could have arranged, without ever needing anyone's belief to make it true. The deliverance happens whether or not the king credits it, whether or not the lepers had reported it, and whether or not the officer ever came to trust it, a reminder that the reality of God's word never depends on how many people are ready to receive it.

crossReferences.note: Foretells the exact horror of siege induced cannibalism now literally fulfilled in Samaria, the outer edge of the covenant curse for persistent unfaithfulness that Moses had warned would fall on a besieged, unrepentant Israel centuries earlier.

Ben-hadad had besieged this same city once before under Ahab, and Israel survived by battle that time, making the total helplessness of this second siege, ended without a single Israelite blow, all the more striking by contrast.

The LORD strikes down an entire Assyrian army besieging Jerusalem in a single night without any human battle, the same pattern of deliverance by divine action alone seen here on a smaller, earlier scale at Samaria.

The identical horror of mothers eating their own children recurs when Jerusalem itself finally falls to Babylon, proving the covenant curse fulfilled here at Samaria was never confined to one city or one generation.

Famine again grips a besieged Israelite capital when Jerusalem finally falls, showing the exact scarcity described here as extreme and unprecedented recurred in the very city that had once witnessed and should have remembered this warning.

Moses tells a trapped, defenceless Israel that the LORD will fight for them and they need only be still, the same total passivity in the face of an impossible threat that marks Israel's rescue from Aram in this passage.

Joseph tells his brothers that God turned a great famine, the same Hebrew word used here, into a great deliverance through the very brothers who had wronged him, another instance of the LORD reversing raab through an unlikely instrument.

The wilderness generation saw the LORD's glory and his signs yet tested him and disobeyed, and none of them were permitted to see the promised land, the same pattern of eyewitness unbelief that costs the scoffing officer his place at the feast.

The LORD promises to open the windows of heaven and pour out blessing without measure on a faithful, tithing people, the same rare word for windows that the officer mockingly assumes could only ever describe an impossible demand rather than a genuine promise.
The LORD of Hosts promises a coming banquet of rich food and aged wine for all peoples, the permanent, universal version of the sudden, local abundance that appears overnight at Samaria's gate.

Jesus warns that many will come from east and west to share the banquet while the sons of the kingdom are shut outside, a warning that echoes the officer who saw the fulfilled promise yet was barred, by his own unbelief, from tasting it.

Warns believers against the kind of unbelief the scoffing officer displayed, seeing God's works with one's own eyes yet failing to trust and so failing to enter into what those works had already promised.

study.oneStory:
This passage sits at the outer edge of what covenant unfaithfulness could bring on God's own people, siege, famine, and the exact cannibalism Moses had warned of centuries earlier, Deuteronomy 28:53-57. That such a horror could be reversed entirely within a single day, at the LORD's word alone, shows a mercy that answers judgment without waiting for judgment to run its natural course or for repentance to come first.

The deliverance itself is discovered and first enjoyed not by the city's leaders but by four men the city had already cast outside its gates, a pattern that recurs throughout Scripture and finds its fullest expression in Christ's own ministry among the poor, the sick, and the excluded. What begins as a story about grain prices turns out to be a small, exact rehearsal of the gospel, abundance given freely, discovered first by the least likely people, who then cannot keep it to themselves.

The one figure the passage refuses to save is the man who saw everything and believed nothing, an officer close enough to the throne to be trusted with the king's own safety, yet unable to trust a plain prophetic word until it was too late to benefit from it. His fate stands as a permanent warning inside a passage otherwise devoted to grace, that nearness to a fulfilled promise is never the same thing as saving faith in it.

The whole passage points forward to a banquet this one only pictures in miniature, a feast of rich food for all peoples that will never again run short, Isaiah 25:6, and a marriage supper to which the poor, the lame, and the excluded are deliberately invited first, Luke 14:21. Samaria's one day of overnight abundance is a signpost toward a feast that will never need to happen twice.

quiz.q: What horrifying extremity did the famine in besieged Samaria drive two women to commit?

options.text: They agreed to boil and eat their own sons in successive days, though the second woman hid her son to avoid her part of the agreement.
options.note: Verses 28 to 29 record this exact horrifying account brought before the king.

options.text: They fled the city together to surrender to the Arameans.
options.note: The text describes a horrifying act of cannibalism within the city, not an escape or surrender.

options.text: They simply requested more grain rations from the king.
options.note: Their appeal to the king concerned this act of cannibalism specifically, a far graver matter than rationing.

options.text: Nothing unusual happened; the city had ample food.
options.note: The text explicitly describes an extreme famine and horrifying acts resulting from it.

quiz.q: What did Elisha prophesy would happen at the gate of Samaria by the next day, and how did the king's officer respond?

options.text: He prophesied famine prices would collapse to ordinary levels within a day, and the officer scoffed that this was impossible even if the LORD made windows in heaven.
options.note: 7:1-2 records both the prophecy and the officer's explicit disbelief.

options.text: He prophesied the siege would continue for another year.
options.note: Elisha prophesied an imminent, drastic reversal within about a day, not continued suffering.

options.text: The officer believed immediately and thanked Elisha.
options.note: The officer explicitly mocked the prophecy as impossible rather than believing it.

options.text: Elisha refused to give any specific prophecy.
options.note: Elisha gave a very specific, dated prophecy about prices at the city gate.

quiz.q: How did the Aramean army come to abandon its camp, and who discovered it first?

options.text: The LORD caused them to hear the sound of a great approaching army and flee in panic, and four lepers, going to surrender or die, discovered the abandoned camp first.
options.note: 7:6-8 records the cause of the flight and the lepers' discovery.

options.text: Israel's army attacked and drove the Arameans out by force.
options.note: No battle occurred; the Arameans fled based on a sound the LORD caused them to hear, without any actual attack.

options.text: The king of Israel personally led a surprise raid on the camp.
options.note: The king was unaware of the abandonment until informed by the lepers' report through the gatekeepers.

options.text: The Arameans never left their camp.
options.note: The text explicitly states they fled at twilight, abandoning tents, horses, and donkeys.

quiz.q: Why did the four lepers decide to report their discovery rather than keep it secret?

options.text: They concluded they were not doing right by staying silent on a day of good news, fearing that delay would bring judgment on them, so they told the king's household.
options.note: Verse 9 records their exact reasoning and resulting decision to report the news.

options.text: They were caught by Aramean soldiers who forced them to confess.
options.note: No soldiers remained to catch them; their decision to report came from their own conscience.

options.text: They wanted to keep all the plunder for themselves permanently.
options.note: Their stated motive was conscience about withholding good news, not securing plunder exclusively for themselves.

options.text: They never reported anything, and the city remained unaware.
options.note: The text explicitly records them reporting to the gatekeepers, who informed the king's household.

quiz.q: How was Elisha's prophecy about prices and about the skeptical officer both fulfilled?

options.text: Prices collapsed to a seah of flour for a shekel exactly as foretold, and the officer, appointed to oversee the gate, was trampled to death by the crowd, seeing the abundance but never eating any of it.
options.note: 7:16-20 records both fulfillments in careful, repeated detail.

options.text: Prices remained high despite Elisha's prophecy.
options.note: The text explicitly states prices fell exactly as Elisha had foretold.

options.text: The officer survived and enjoyed the abundance himself.
options.note: The officer was trampled to death and explicitly did not eat any of the food, precisely as prophesied.

options.text: Neither part of the prophecy came true.
options.note: Both the pricing collapse and the officer's death are recorded as exact fulfillments of Elisha's words.

questions: Samaria's siege reduced people to unthinkable horror, yet the LORD's deliverance came suddenly and completely. What situation in your life feels too far gone for God to turn around, and how does this account challenge that assumption?

The officer saw the very door to belief opened by Elisha's clear prophecy, yet mocked it, and it cost him everything. Where might skepticism be keeping you from receiving a promise or provision God has clearly set before you?

The lepers, the very people society had cast out, were the first to discover and enjoy God's abundant provision. How does it change your view of yourself, or others, to know God often reveals His grace first to the overlooked and excluded?

The lepers felt they could not keep the good news to themselves, even though silence would have benefited them personally. What good news has God given you that you are tempted to keep to yourself rather than share?

The LORD delivered Samaria with no human battle at all, defeating an army with sound alone. Where do you need to trust God to work in a situation where you feel completely powerless to change anything yourself?

translationNotes.note: The famine prices recorded, a donkey's head for eighty shekels and a small measure of dove's dung for five shekels, reflect the collapse of ordinary food supply to the point that normally inedible or unclean items became traded commodities.

A seah, roughly 7.3 liters, of fine flour selling for a single shekel represents an extraordinary return to ordinary, even generous, pre-famine pricing, making Elisha's prophecy strikingly specific and easily falsifiable if untrue.

The Arameans' assumption that Israel had hired the kings of the Hittites and Egyptians reflects real geopolitical anxieties of the era, showing how a supernatural sound was interpreted through entirely natural, plausible fears.
